newsitem.title: JAPAN: Fujitsu to boost 64-megabit computer chip output.
newsitem.headline: Fujitsu to boost 64-megabit computer chip output.

text.p: Major Japanese microchip maker Fujitsu Ltd said on Tuesday it plans to raise its output of next-generation 64-megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips, encouraged by demand from personal computer makers.

Fujitsu now plans to make 1.5 million 64-megabit chips per month by the end of the 1997/98 business year, up from its September forecast of one million for that fiscal year, which ends on March 31, a Fujitsu spokeswoman said.

"An increasing number of PCs are using 64-megabit DRAMs," a Fujitsu spokeswoman said, adding the company thinks that demand will shift from 16-megabit DRAMs to 64-megabit chips at a faster pace than it initially expected.

The most widely used industry chip is the 16-megabit DRAM, but falling prices have forced many semiconductor makers to lower their production plans for that chip and revise down planned investment in their semiconductor business.
Fujitsu said last month that it had joined other chip makers like NEC Corp, Toshiba Corp and Mitsubishi Electric Corp in boosting production of 64-megabit DRAMs.
It said at that time it would start mass production of 64-megabit DRAMs at its Iwate plant in northern Japan early next year, six months sooner than originally planned.
Fujitsu also said its new U.S. plant in Oregon will start making the same chips in late 1997.
The price of the 16-megabit DRAM chip fell sharply this year and was one-fifth of its January level in August.
The price fall was due to an unexpected slowdown in PC sales worldwide and oversupply of the chips.

Last week, however, the Nihon Keizai Shimbun economic daily said overseas spot prices of 16-megabit DRAM chips were sharply recovering, reaching $12 to $15 per unit which was almost double its price at the beginning of September.
The paper said that the price rises were due to inventory adjustments at personal computer makers and smaller shipments by chip makers.
